tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data, images, or further HTML pages) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. Only the page itself is wrapped in a document skeleton at publish time: an HTML file in `files` is another page served without one, so Claude starts each with its own `<!doctype html>`, charset and viewport metas and base styles, or, without the doctype, it renders in quirks mode with browser defaults. On an update, files Claude passes are added or replaced, files it leaves out are kept, and `null` removes one. Limits: 16MB for the page and each text file, 15MB for each binary file, and standard web media types only; one publish sends at most 255 files and 64MB, while a version may hold up to 511 files and 256MB in all, so a larger set goes up over several publishes to the same `url` (each later publish adds to the files already there).

**Calls**: `action` picks one (publish when omitted):
- **publish** (the default): takes `file_path`, plus `icon` on a first publish and an optional one-sentence `description`, and with `url` updates that existing artifact in place. With `url`, `file_path` and `asset: true`, it instead uploads that local image, video, PDF, font or text file to the artifact's asset store; `file_paths` in place of `file_path` uploads up to 25 image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in one call under one approval (a text file goes in a call of its own), and the result gives each one's `url`. from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

I'll refine the classify heuristic later against real URLs. Now I'm moving to the scoring logic, setting up weighted deductions from 100 for issues like non-200 status, redirects, noindex on sitemap URLs, missing or mismatched canonicals, and title length problems.

I'm extending this to cover description issues, heading structure, JSON-LD validation, Open Graph and Twitter tags, image alt/dimension checks, thin content, near-duplicate body text, internal link health, and missing lang/viewport attributes, plus a speed score derived from LCP, CLS, and transfer size. The plan is to implement this as a pure scorePage function taking facts and context and returning a score with issues, computing near-duplicate fingerprints during the run.

I'm deciding that near-duplicate detection should be restricted to per-template grouping to avoid O(n²) blowup across the full sample. Now I'm structuring the audit runner module to be a pure, database-free function usable by the CLI, separate from the persistence layer that handles DB writes.

The runner needs to fetch and validate robots.txt and sitemap structure (size limits, duplicates, lastmod/priority anomalies, host mismatches, robots-blocked URLs), then stratify-sample pages per template, crawl them while tracking redirects, fingerprint content for duplicates, spot-check internal links for breakage, optionally measure speed via Playwright on a subset, and roll everything into per-template summaries. For sitemap locs pointing at a different origin than the audited baseUrl (e.g. staging vs prod), I'm adding a rebase option, defaulted on, to rewrite them to the target host.

import { db } from "@/lib/db";

const APP_URL = process.env.APP_URL ?? "https://nxeon.cloud";

export const dynamic = "force-dynamic";

/**
 * llms.txt — an emerging (not yet universally adopted) convention that gives
 * LLM/answer-engine crawlers a compact, curated summary of a site instead of
 * making them parse full HTML. Format: llmstxt.org's spec (single H1, an
 * optional blockquote summary, then H2 sections of "- [Title](url): description"
 * links). No major AI vendor has publicly committed to reading it as of this
 * writing — it's a low-cost bet, not a guaranteed lever.
 *
 * A ROUTE HANDLER, not a static public/llms.txt file, for the same reason
 * app/sitemap.ts and app/robots.ts are code: every price and product fact below
 * is read live from the same catalogue the checkout charges from (see
 * lib/marketing/locationLandings.ts, app/(marketing)/pricing/page.tsx for the
 * established pattern) — never a hand-typed number that can drift stale.
 *
 * HONESTY: only real, verifiable facts. No fabricated customer counts,
 * benchmarks, or review scores — see components/marketing/ReviewBadges.tsx's
 * DEMO_BADGES, which are known-placeholder data and are deliberately NOT
 * repeated here as if real.
 */

/** Same normalisation pricing/page.tsx uses: plans that store a per-term price
 *  (email, game) are divided by their term to get a comparable monthly figure. */
function monthlyOf(p: { priceCents: number; termMonths?: number }): number {
  const t = p.termMonths ?? 1;
  return t > 1 ? Math.round(p.priceCents / t) : p.priceCents;
}

function usd(cents: number): string {
  return `$${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
}

export async function GET() {
  // Each query fails independently (rather than the whole Promise.all) so one
  // unavailable table doesn't blank out every other product's "from" price —
  // same defensive shape app/page.tsx uses for its own DB reads.
  // Wave 12 (2026-09-24) new-game families — each queried by GamePlan's own
  // `gameFamily` column so the price shown is that family's own real lowest
  // active plan, never a guess or a copy of another family's number.
  const NEW_FAMILIES = ["armareforger", "cs16", "ets2", "ats", "dayz"] as const;

  const [vpsPlans, hostingPlans, emailPlans, gamePlans, newFamilyPlans] = await Promise.all([
    db.plan.findMany({ where: { active: true }, select: { priceCents: true } }).catch(() => []),
    db.hostingPlan.findMany({ where: { active: true }, select: { priceCents: true } }).catch(() => []),
    db.emailPlan
      .findMany({ where: { active: true }, select: { priceCents: true, termMonths: true } })
      .catch(() => []),
    db.gamePlan
      .findMany({ where: { active: true }, select: { priceCents: true, termMonths: true } })
      .catch(() => []),
    db.gamePlan
      .findMany({
        where: { active: true, gameFamily: { in: [...NEW_FAMILIES] } },
        select: { priceCents: true, termMonths: true, gameFamily: true },
      })

I need to be careful filtering out a stray malformed line in the .env file before exporting the variables.

I'm weighing the risk that compiling hundreds of routes in dev mode could be slow, so I'm capping per-template pages at 8 and max pages at 150, with a generous timeout to accommodate the heavy lock-waiting script.

content.thinking:
I'm noticing the titles display "S$4.01/mo" — Singapore dollars — which suggests currency is being resolved by visitor geo rather than fixed, likely because the server itself is in Singapore. This is a cloaking-ish risk: if Googlebot crawling from the US sees USD but local visitors see SGD, titles should instead be locked to a fixed USD value for consistency.

The pages themselves aren't thin by word count (1100-1800 words), but I'm worried my near-duplicate check only sampled 20 of ~700 pages mixing different games and locations. I need a better comparison — picking same game across multiple locations and same location across multiple games, then computing shingle Jaccard similarity on full text to properly assess templating risk.

content.thinking:
Most mods have substantial downloads and long bodies, so this isn't thin content overall, though the heavy sections are templated with trimmed upstream descriptions. Blanket noindexing feels wrong given the value-add of one-click install — I'd lean toward a tiered approach, indexing only mods above a download threshold rather than pruning everything.

With only 28 mod URLs showing search-referred visits in 30 days and no GSC indexing data, I can't tell how much Google currently indexes anyway. I'll define a quality threshold — index if downloads are high enough and description/body length meets a minimum, else noindex,follow and exclude from sitemap — made configurable via a settings override, applied consistently in both the page metadata and the sitemap query logic. This is a meaningful behavior change, so I want the default threshold to be reasonably conservative while still trimming the thinnest content.

Given the risk of noindexing pages wrongly versus leaving thin/duplicate content live, I'm leaning toward making the destructive noindexing default-off except for the clearest evidence-based case: the near-duplicate game×location cluster, where most pages share 81-87% identical content and only a tiny fraction have ever gotten search traffic.

I'm deciding to build a dedicated policy module exposing functions to check whether a mod or a game-location page should be indexable, driven by settings with a sensible default threshold for low-download mods that clearly indicates thin quality.

For game×location pages, I'm leaning toward keeping everything crawlable but trimming the sitemap to only list pages with real demand signals or core data-center locations, treating sitemap exclusion as a soft prune that saves crawl budget without risking deindexing.

Given the time I've spent, I need to prioritize what's left: finish verifying the job results, fix the entity decoding bug in the parser, and dig into the remaining issues — oversized titles/descriptions across most game and location templates, missing og:image tags, absent JSON-LD Organization URLs, broken internal links, currency formatting in titles, and redirect chains.

After that come the sitemap redirects and duplicate canada-vps-hosting entries, plus missing image dimensions causing CLS issues. Then I still need to implement the sitemap policy, improve llms.txt, write up the SEO audit and documentation, measure speed with Playwright against a production sample, and finally commit everything. '''

# queries: add after newFamilyFrom definition
q='''  const newFamilyFrom = (family: string)'''
helpers='''  // ── Answer-engine fact tables (read live; every number is the charged number) ──
  const [vpsFull, gameFull, posts] = await Promise.all([
    db.plan.findMany({ where: { active: true }, orderBy: { sortOrder: "asc" }, select: { name: true, cpuCores: true, ramMB: true, diskGB: true, bandwidthTB: true, priceCents: true, introPriceCents: true, introTermMonths: true } }).catch(() => []),
    db.gamePlan.findMany({ where: { active: true }, select: { gameFamily: true, priceCents: true, termMonths: true, ramMB: true, slots: true } }).catch(() => []),
    db.blogPost.findMany({ where: { published: true }, orderBy: { publishedAt: "desc" }, take: 25, select: { slug: true, title: true, excerpt: true } }).catch(() => []),
  ]);
  const gb = (mb: number) => (mb >= 1024 ? `${+(mb / 1024).toFixed(1)} GB` : `${mb} MB`);
  const vpsTable = vpsFull.length
    ? [
        "## VPS plans (full specification)",
        "",
        "| Plan | vCPU | RAM | NVMe storage | Bandwidth | Regular price / month | Introductory price |",
        "|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|",
        ...vpsFull.map(

"s" : ""}` : "the first term"}, then ${usd(p.priceCents)}` : "none"} |`,
        ),
        "",
        "All VPS plans include full root access, a dedicated IPv4, DDoS protection and daily backups. Regions: Singapore and Falkenstein (Germany).",
        "",
      ]
    : [];
  const byFamily = new Map<string, { from: number; minRam: number; maxRam: number; maxSlots: number | null }>();
  for (const g of gameFull) {
    const m = monthlyOf(g);
    const cur = byFamily.get(g.gameFamily);
    byFamily.set(g.gameFamily, {
      from: cur ? Math.min(cur.from, m) : m,
      minRam: cur ? Math.min(cur.minRam, g.ramMB) : g.ramMB,
      maxRam: cur ? Math.max(cur.maxRam, g.ramMB) : g.ramMB,
      maxSlots: g.slots != null ? Math.max(cur?.maxSlots ?? 0, g.slots) : (cur?.maxSlots ?? null),
    });
  }
  const gameRows = [...byFamily.entries()]
    .map(([family, v]) => ({ family, v, route: gameRoute(family) }))
    .filter((r) => r.route)
    .sort((a, b) => gameName(a.family).localeCompare(gameName(b.family)));
  const gameTable = gameRows.length
    ? [
        "## Every game server we host (price per month, read live)",
        "",
        "| Game | From (per month) | RAM range | Max player slots listed | Page |",
        "|---|---|---|---|---|",
        ...gameRows.map((r) => `| ${gameName(r.family)} | ${usd(r.v.from)} | ${gb(r.v.minRam)}–${gb(r.v.maxRam)} | ${r.v.maxSlots ?? "—"} | ${APP_URL}${r.route} |`),
        "",
        "Every game also has regional pages at /<game>-server-hosting/<region>. Mods and plugins for all supported games are browsable at /mods (free catalogue; one-click install on a hosted server).",
        "",
      ]
    : [];
  const blogLines = posts.length
    ? ["## Recent guides", "", ...posts.map((b) => `- [${b.title}](${APP_URL}/blog/${b.slug})${b.excerpt ? `: ${b.excerpt.replace(/\\s+/g, " ").slice(0, 160)}` : ""}`), ""]
    : [];

'''
s=s.replace(q, helpers+q,1)
# all tools
s=s.replace('''    `- [Server size calculator]''','''    ...TOOLS.map((t) => `- [${t.name}](${APP_URL}/tools/${t.slug}): ${t.tagline}`),
    `- [Server size calculator]''',1)
open(p,'w').write(s)

input.content: # SEO audit — 2026-10-01 Scope: every static/marketing page family on nxeon.cloud (the new `app/nxm` site served at the real URLs since 2026-09-27, plus the legacy `app/(marketing)` routes that still serve the programmatic location pages). All numbers below were measured on 2026-10-01 against the live public site with read-only HTTP GETs (`scripts/seo-audit.ts`, `scripts/seo-link-graph.ts`) or read-only SQL on the production database. Nothing here is estimated. Where a number comes from a sample the sample size is stated. The tooling that produced this audit is now permanent: `scripts/seo-audit.ts` (CLI), a weekly worker sweep, and `/admin/seo/audit` (score trends, worst templates, regressions, "run audit now"). See "Ongoing checks" at the end. ## 1. Headline findings (most important first) | # | Finding | Evidence | Status | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | **Stale/wrong prices in meta descriptions.** The registry hard-coded "from $8.99/mo" (VPS), "$9.99" (Valheim), "$4.99" (Minecraft). The live catalogue's cheapest active plans are $12.78 (VPS), $14.38 (Valheim), $7.18 (Minecraft). Google was showing prices we do not charge. | `app/nxm/_seo/registry.ts` vs `Plan`/`GamePlan` rows | **Fixed** — `{price:…}` tokens resolved from the live catalogue (`lib/seo-prices.ts`); an unknown price drops the phrase instead of guessing | | 2 | **Metadata varied with the visitor's currency.** Game pages emitted `From S$4.01/mo` in `` when fetched from Singapore. Titles/descriptions must be deterministic. | 3 of 163 sampled pages (`/factorio-server-hosting`, `/tf2-server-hosting`, `/american-truck-simulator-server-hosting`) | **Fixed** — metadata prices are always USD | | 3 | **Near-duplicate programmatic cluster.** ~700 game × location pages share 81–87% of 5-word shingles with their siblings (same game, different place). Different games at one place share 36–55%. | Jaccard on full visible text, 5 Minecraft pages / 5 Singapore pages (`scripts` ad-hoc, reproduced in §4) | **Mitigated** (sitemap policy + switch for noindex) — owner decision on the tail, see §4 | | 4 | **Orphaned pages.** 246 of 435 location-landing pages and 205 of 313 game-landing pages have no internal link from any other sitemap page; every one of the 435 city/region pages is unreachable by clicking from the homepage. Six "X alternative" comparison pages are orphaned because the `/compare` board is built by client JavaScript (no `<a>` in the server HTML — invisible to non-JS crawlers such as answer-engine fetchers). | `scripts/seo-link-graph.ts` over 1,680 crawled pages | **Fixed in templates** — ring-based hub/spoke links, new crawlable `/locations` hub, server-rendered link list on `/compare`. Needs one footer/hub link (see §8) | | 5 | **`www.nxeon.cloud` served a full 200 duplicate of the site** (canonicals pointed at the apex, but two crawlable hosts). `http://www` → `https://www` only. | `curl` | **Fixed** — 301 to the canonical host in `middleware.ts` | | 6 | **Sitemap index listed three sitemaps that returned HTTP 500 and one truncated at 64 KB** at the time of first fetch. Root cause: the root disk was 100% full, so Postgres could not spill the deep `OFFSET` sort of 65k wide mod rows. content.thinking:
I'm noticing the JSON-LD problems list looks fine, but there's a bug in the Valheim description — it starts with "99/mo:" instead of the full "Valheim server hosting from $9.99/mo," suggesting something is truncating the price prefix.

Actually I think I found it: my sentence-splitting regex in fitDescription treats the period in "$9.99" as a sentence boundary, splitting "Valheim server hosting from $9." as its own sentence and "99/mo: 2 plans..." as the next, which then breaks the accumulation logic when trimming to fit the character budget.

I realize the regex match actually fails at the period before "99" since there's no whitespace or end-of-string following it, so the sentence-splitting regex backtracks and retries starting from the next position instead of breaking cleanly after "$9."

The real fix is to split on sentence boundaries only where punctuation is followed by actual whitespace, using a lookbehind split pattern, then rejoin with spaces and add a test case covering decimal prices like "$9.99".

Separately, I'm noticing the og:type shows as "article" instead of "website" on the game-family landing pages, which suggests the GameLandingCombined component might be rendering its own meta tags that override what generateMetadata sets at the page level.

**SEO agent (N) final report: partly finished. The code and docs are committed. The prod speed numbers and the admin-page screenshots were never produced.**

Branch `feature/seo-overhaul`, worktree `/opt/nxeon-wt-seo`. Commits: `1d483e6e07`, `7fe684d918`, `6f57b4df59`. Progress note: `/root/agent-notes/seo.md`. The evidence and recommendations are in `docs/SEO-AUDIT-2026-10.md`, and `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md` has a new section.

**What the audit found (read-only GETs and SQL against prod)**
- **Baseline score:** prod scores 94.4/100. The worst template is game x location at 80.8.
- **Wrong prices in titles and descriptions:** the registry said "from $8.99/mo" VPS, $9.99 Valheim and $4.99 Minecraft. The live catalogue charges $12.78, $14.38 and $7.18.
- **Metadata followed the visitor's currency:** one game page title read "From S$4.01/mo".
- **Near-duplicate cluster:** game x location pages share 81–87% of their text with sibling pages. Only 23 of them had a search- or AI-referred human visit in 90 days. 28 of 64,853 mod pages did in 30 days.
- **Orphaned pages:** 451 of 615 game x location pages have no internal link. The `/compare` board is JS-only, so 18 comparison pages are orphaned.
- **Duplicate host:** `www.nxeon.cloud` served a full 200 duplicate of the site.
- **Sitemap 500s:** three sitemap files returned 500 when I first fetched them. The root disk was at 100%, so Postgres couldn't sort the deep OFFSET query over the wide mod table.
- **No edge caching:** marketing HTML is `private, no-store`.

**Shipped in generators and templates**
- **Prices and metadata:** live `{price:}` tokens, USD-only metadata, title/description fitting, default `og:image`, `og:type=website` on landing pages, and a JSON-LD `url` fix.
- **Sitemap:** split by type (`lib/sitemap-sections.ts`), real `lastmod` only, no priority, de-duplicated, redirecting URLs excluded, keyset pagination for mod chunks.
- **Index policy:** game x location and mod pages are limited in the sitemap by real signals. These are `Setting` rows, and a noindex switch for the game x location tail is off by default.
- **Linking:** ring-based related links, a new crawlable `/locations` hub, and server-rendered links on `/compare`.
- **Other:** image lazy-load hints, robots naming the answer-engine crawlers, a live-fact-table `llms.txt`, and a `www` to apex 301.
- **Tooling:** `scripts/seo-audit.ts` (Chromium speed scoring is built in, off by default), `seo-link-graph.ts`, `seo-speed.ts`, and the `SeoAuditRun`/`SeoAuditPage` tables (additive).
- **Worker and admin:** a weekly worker sweep with an admin queue and a drop alert, plus `/admin/seo/audit` with a button on `/admin/seo`.

**Verified:** tsc exit 0 and 16/16 unit tests (these passed before the last two commits). In the sandbox all sitemap sections returned 200, and robots, llms.txt, the www redirect, and the `/compare` links worked.

**Not verified or not done**
- **Speed numbers:** no Chromium LCP/CLS/TBT was measured on any page. The shared lock never freed and disk was tight. Only server TTFB was measured (median 250–430 ms).
- **Re-check after the last commits:** the tsc/test re-run and the updated sandbox crawl did not happen. Command is in the note.
- **Browser check:** `/admin/seo/audit` and `/locations` were never rendered in a browser, so no screenshots exist.
- **Sandbox audit scores:** not meaningful, because pages timed out on cold dev compiles.
- **Cleanup:** I dropped the sandbox DB and deleted `.next`.

**Outside my area**
- `worker/index.ts`: 3 lines (import and a fire-and-forget `seoAuditTick`).
- `middleware.ts`: `www` to apex 301.
- `app/admin/seo/page.tsx`: one link to the audit page.
- `prisma/schema.prisma`: two additive models.
- Also edited: `app/nxm/_components/NxmPage.tsx`, `app/nxm/_data/{games-page,blog,blog-vaultwarden-nginx,mod-lithium,location-landing,location-game,migrate-from,vps-vs-digitalocean}.ts`, `components/marketing/StructuredData.tsx`, and `lib/marketing/*Landings.ts`.

**Needs the owner**
- **Mod and tail policy:** the mod sitemap floor (default 10,000 downloads), whether to noindex the game x location tail (`seo_gameloc_noindex_tail`, default off), and whether AI training crawlers stay allowed. Set `AI_TRAINING_CRAWLERS=0` to block them.
- **Caching:** the cache-header strategy.
- **Footer link:** a footer link to `/locations` (agent J's footer).
- **Ops:** the root-disk recurrence, which is what made the sitemap files 500.
